revisions.title: The whole city becomes a school
revisions.body: Protagoras presents virtue as a civic practice learned from earliest childhood: everyone must share in it, and the nurse, mother, paidagogos, and father teach through oppositions such as just and unjust. The school-like pattern extends beyond one specialist; it names the roles and repeated instruction through which the city forms its children.

revisions.title: Pleasure, pain, and the measuring art
revisions.body: The inquiry first tests whether pleasure itself is good, after Protagoras distinguishes pleasant and painful things that may be good, bad, or neutral. Socrates then turns to knowledge: the question is whether knowledge can rule rather than be dragged by pleasure or pain. The measuring art therefore joins pleasure and pain to a problem of comparison and ignorance, without recasting the sequence as immediate appearance versus future consequence.
